title: Physiotherapy in Nursing Care
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Musculoskeletal Injuries

headings.title: Introduction to Physiotherapy in Nursing
headings.content: Physiotherapy in nursing care represents a vital dimension of holistic patient management, focusing on restoring physical function, enhancing mobility, and preventing secondary complications during illness or recovery. Nurses and physiotherapists share a common goal: improving patient outcomes through comprehensive care strategies. While physical therapists design specific rehabilitation regimens, nurses are at the bedside 24 hours a day, uniquely positioned to reinforce these exercises, monitor patient tolerance, and integrate mobility goals into routine daily living activities. Understanding physiotherapy principles allows nursing students in Nigeria to bridge the gap between acute medical treatment and long-term functional independence. In many healthcare settings, nurses must recognize early signs of physical decline, such as muscle weakness or joint stiffness, and intervene proactively. Collaboration between nursing and physiotherapy ensures that patients recovering from strokes, orthopedic surgeries, or prolonged bedrest receive continuous, coordinated care. Furthermore, incorporating basic physical therapy concepts into nursing practice empowers patients to participate actively in their healing process, shortening hospital stays and reducing the incidence of hospital-acquired complications like pressure ulcers and deep vein thrombosis.

headings.title: Goals and Objectives of Therapeutic Exercises
headings.content: Therapeutic exercises are fundamental components of patient rehabilitation, designed to address specific physical deficits and restore optimal bodily function. The primary goals of these exercises include improving muscle strength, enhancing joint flexibility, increasing endurance, and restoring coordination and balance. For nursing students, recognizing the categorization of these exercises is essential. Passive range of motion exercises are performed by the nurse or therapist for patients who cannot move independently, helping to maintain joint flexibility and prevent contractures without patient muscle exertion. Active-assisted exercises involve partial patient effort with support from the caregiver, encouraging muscle engagement while ensuring safety. Active exercises are performed entirely by the patient against gravity or resistance, promoting significant gains in muscle strength and cardiovascular endurance. Specific objectives also target respiratory function, such as deep breathing and coughing exercises that prevent atelectasis in immobilized patients. By understanding these goals, nurses can accurately assess patient progress, report deviations to the multidisciplinary team, and tailor daily nursing interventions to support the patient's ongoing physical rehabilitation journey.

headings.title: Types of Physiotherapy Modalities in Patient Care
headings.content: Physiotherapy modalities encompass a wide array of physical agents and technical tools used to manage pain, reduce inflammation, and accelerate tissue healing. Nurses frequently encounter and assist with these modalities in various clinical settings. Thermal modalities, such as cryotherapy (cold application) and thermotherapy (heat application), are widely used; cold reduces acute inflammation and numbs localized pain, while heat promotes vasodilation, relaxes muscle spasms, and improves local blood circulation. Electrical stimulation units, such as Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS), are commonly employed for pain management by blocking pain signals traveling to the spinal cord. Ultrasound therapy utilizes high-frequency sound waves to generate deep thermal effects in soft tissues, helping to break down scar tissue and enhance healing in chronic tendinopathies. Traction techniques, applied manually or mechanically, help decompress spinal discs and relieve nerve root compression in patients with chronic back pain. Understanding these modalities enables nurses to monitor patients for adverse effects, such as skin burns or excessive skin irritation, and ensures that nursing care complements the physical therapy treatment plan safely and effectively.

headings.title: The Nurse's Role in Assisting with Mobility and Ambulation
headings.content: Assisting patients with mobility and ambulation is a core nursing responsibility that directly influences recovery speed and independence. Bed mobility includes turning, repositioning, and moving a patient from lying to sitting, which requires proper body mechanics to protect both the patient and the nurse from injury. When transitioning a patient to ambulation, nurses must first assess the patient's baseline stability, vital signs, and cognitive awareness. Orthostatic hypotension is a common risk when patients stand up after prolonged bedrest, requiring nurses to allow the patient to dangle their legs at the bedside before attempting to stand. Assistive devices such as walkers, crutches, and canes must be correctly sized and fitted for the patient, and the nurse must understand the specific gait pattern associated with each device. For instance, when using a walker, the patient typically moves the walker forward first, followed by the affected leg, and then the unaffected leg. Safety is paramount; nurses should use gait belts, ensure clear pathways free of clutter, and provide adequate physical support during initial ambulation attempts. Documenting distance walked, patient tolerance, and any signs of fatigue or dizziness ensures continuity of care and informs the multidisciplinary team of functional progress.

headings.title: Positioning and Preventing Musculoskeletal Complications
headings.content: Proper positioning is critical in preventing severe musculoskeletal and integumentary complications in immobilized patients. Prolonged immobility places patients at high risk for pressure ulcers, foot drop, contractures, and muscle atrophy. Nurses must implement a strict repositioning schedule, typically turning patients every two hours, while utilizing pillows, wedge cushions, and foam pads to relieve pressure over bony prominences. Correct alignment of the spine, hips, and limbs is vital; for example, trochanter rolls prevent external rotation of the hips, and footboards or specialized splints prevent plantar flexion, commonly known as foot drop. In addition, the use of therapeutic specialty mattresses can significantly reduce interface pressure. Nursing assessments should include daily checks of skin integrity, joint range of motion, and signs of deep vein thrombosis, such as unilateral calf swelling or tenderness. Educating family members on the importance of these positioning techniques ensures continuity of care when nursing staff are not present. By maintaining proper anatomical alignment and mitigating pressure points, nurses preserve functional joint range and protect vulnerable tissues from ischemic damage.

headings.title: Collaborative Care: Working with Physical Therapists
headings.content: Collaborative care between nurses and physical therapists is essential for achieving seamless, patient-centered rehabilitation. Effective interprofessional communication bridges the gap between acute medical management and restorative functional therapy. Nurses observe the patient's daily responses to pain, fatigue, and environmental stressors, providing critical feedback to the physical therapist regarding the patient's real-time functional capacity. Conversely, physical therapists share detailed exercise protocols and safety guidelines with the nursing staff, enabling nurses to reinforce these therapies during evening and night shifts. Interdisciplinary team meetings offer a platform to discuss patient progress, address barriers to rehabilitation, and adjust goals collaboratively. For instance, if a patient experiences severe morning joint stiffness, the nurse can coordinate pain medication administration with the physical therapy session schedule to maximize patient comfort and participation. Mutual respect and clear delineation of roles prevent duplication of effort and reduce confusion for the patient and their family. Ultimately, this collaborative synergy accelerates recovery, enhances safety, and ensures that the patient's holistic rehabilitation needs are consistently met throughout their healthcare journey.

headings.title: Patient Education and Safe Discharge Planning
headings.content: Patient education and safe discharge planning are critical final steps in ensuring sustained recovery and preventing hospital readmissions. Discharge planning must begin early in the admission process, involving the patient, their family caregivers, and the multidisciplinary team. Nurses play a leading role in educating patients on home exercise routines, proper body mechanics, and the safe use of assistive devices like crutches, walkers, or wheelchairs. Education must be tailored to the patient's cognitive level, cultural background, and physical capabilities, often utilizing verbal instructions, demonstrations, and written or pictorial take-home guides. Furthermore, nurses must assess the patient's home environment for potential hazards, such as loose rugs, poor lighting, or blocked pathways, and recommend necessary modifications like installing bathroom grab bars or ramps. Providing information on warning signs—such as severe pain, sudden swelling, or worsening mobility—empowers patients to seek timely medical attention. A well-executed discharge plan bridges the hospital-to-home transition, fosters patient self-reliance, and supports long-term health and functional independence within the community.
